analysis.one_liner: Lets workers take sexual harassment and sex discrimination cases to court instead of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 38 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a vote, sitting in the House Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers are hired, they are often required to sign a form agreeing that any future dispute — including sexual harassment and sex discrimination — will be settled in private arbitration rather than court. This bill would void those clauses for sex discrimination disputes, so workers could sue in open court, decide the issue in front of a judge rather than an arbitrator, and have cases that are not hidden behind closed doors. Union contracts negotiated by labor organizations were exempted.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who sign pre-employment arbitration agreements as a condition of getting a job, especially those facing sexual harassment or sex discrimination on the job. They would regain access to public court records, a judge rather than a private arbitrator to decide if the agreement applies, and the leverage of public proceedings.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a predispute arbitration agreement from being valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of a sex discrimination dispute [S2].
Puts the decision about whether the ban applies in the hands of a court rather than the arbitrator, even when the challenge is buried among other contract terms [S3].
Defines the covered disputes broadly to include any conduct that could support a sex-based claim under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, whether or not a formal violation is alleged [S3].
Preserves employees' right to go to court to enforce constitutional and statutory rights even where a collective bargaining agreement contains an arbitration provision [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that require arbitration clauses, which would lose the private forum for sex discrimination claims — a forum that keeps proceedings confidential and avoids jury exposure. Private arbitration providers would also lose that stream of disputes.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue arbitration is faster and less costly for workers than court litigation, and that removing it raises legal expenses that get passed through [S3] (the bill exempts only union collective bargaining agreements, leaving its effects concentrated on nonunion workplaces).

The bill covers only sex discrimination disputes, not discrimination based on race, disability, or other protected categories, and not the broader range of employment claims forced into arbitration, so it fixes only part of the problem [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — restoring public court access for sexual harassment and sex discrimination claims that employers routinely force into confidential arbitration — is substantial for workers. The costs fall mostly on employers in the form of jury exposure and public litigation, and on arbitration providers. The strongest good-faith objection, that arbitration can be faster and cheaper, is partially addressed by letting courts rather than arbitrators decide whether the ban applies. The main design weakness is its narrow scope: it leaves other forms of discrimination and most employment disputes subject to forced arbitration.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late December 2017, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never got a markup or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Cheri Bustos introduced the bill with three original cosponsors across party lines — Reps. Walter Jones (R), Elise Stefanik (R), and Pramila Jayapal (D) — on December 26, 2017 [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On January 22, 2018 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, and no further action was taken [S5].
It accumulated 38 cosponsors, 8 Republicans and 30 Democrats, but the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without a vote in either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that require arbitration clauses kept their ability to push sexual harassment and sex discrimination claims into confidential private arbitration, and arbitration providers kept that business. Workers kept having to sign away their day in court as a condition of employment.

for.name: Rep. Cheri Bustos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties

for.name: Reps. Walter Jones and Elise Stefanik
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, making the bill bipartisan from day one

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never brought it to a markup or vote; it sat at the subcommittee level for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor despite its bipartisan cosponsorship

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from introduction — three of the four original cosponsors signed alongside a Democrat, and the bill finished with 8 Republican and 30 Democratic cosponsors [S3, S4] — so its death in committee was not a party-line vote but a committee decision.

industries.note: The bill would strip employers of their ability to force sex discrimination claims into confidential private arbitration, ending a practice that keeps harassment allegations out of public court records and away from juries. This is precisely the interest the bill was designed to override.
The bill would eliminate a significant stream of employment disputes that are currently routed to private arbitrators. Its income depends on the practice the bill bans.
